title: Pawlikowski’s ‘Fatherland’ and the myth of the good German
gist: A review of Pawel Pawlikowski's film Fatherland, which follows Thomas Mann's 1949 return to Germany and argues it dismantles the myth of the 'good German' by showing a country still covering its wartime tracks.

insights.claim: Pawlikowski's Fatherland, which won the best director award at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, follows Thomas Mann's 1949 visit to Weimar for the Goethe National Prize and completes a loose post-war Europe trilogy with Ida and Cold War.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Awards momentum and a 23 October UK release make it a cultural talking point.

insights.claim: The reviewer reads the film as an unforgiving challenge to the 'good Germany' idea, showing postwar elites such as Gruendgens and the Wagner grandsons covering up their wartime roles.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Reflects continuing cultural debate on German collective memory.

insights.claim: Pawlikowski's method of starting from people and relationships so that history comes alive is the stated approach behind his films.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.quote: If you start with people and relationships, and their situation, suddenly history comes alive
insights.locator: I don’t start with wanting to say something
